content: Extended cycle combined oral contraceptive pills (COCPs) are specifically designed to reduce or eliminate the withdrawal bleeding that typically occurs every 28 days with traditional COCP regimens. Similarly, other combined hormonal contraceptives, which contain both an estrogen and a progestogen, can also be used in extended or continuous cycles. For instance, the vaginal ring NuvaRing has been studied for extended cycle use, and the monthly injection Lunelle may also eliminate bleeding. When a woman takes COCPs, the hormones in the pills suppress ovulation and prevent the shedding of the endometrium, which is the process of menstruation. Traditional COCPs are packaged with 21 active pills containing hormones and 7 placebo pills. During the placebo week, withdrawal bleeding occurs, mimicking a typical 28-day menstrual cycle. However, the placebo pills are not necessary for pregnancy prevention. With monophasic COCPs, the placebo pills can be skipped, allowing the user to move directly to the next pack of active pills, thereby preventing withdrawal bleeding. Skipping placebo pills with bi-phasic or tri-phasic pills still provides pregnancy protection, but the abrupt change in hormone levels may lead to irregular spotting or bleeding. Recently, several pharmaceutical companies have received FDA approval to package COCPs specifically for the purpose of reducing the frequency of or completely eliminating withdrawal bleeding. Extended or continuous use of COCPs has been employed for many years to manage conditions such as endometriosis, dysmenorrhea, and symptoms associated with menstruation. Some studies suggest that women who experience premenstrual-type symptoms during the placebo week of traditional COCP regimens may experience significantly fewer symptoms when using extended cycle COCPs. More recently, personal preference to avoid menstruation has become a common reason for using extended cycle regimens. Among adolescents, personal preference is the most frequent reason for prescribing extended cycle or continuous use COCPs. Satisfaction with contraceptive methods, adherence to taking pills on time, and discontinuation rates do not differ significantly between traditional and extended cycle regimens. The most common side effect of extended cycle COCPs is breakthrough bleeding, although this tends to decrease over time. In a 12-month study of a continuous COCP regimen, 59% of women experienced no bleeding between months six and twelve, and 79% of women experienced no bleeding by month twelve. One of the early extended cycle COCPs, Seasonale, was marketed with the slogan, Fewer periods. More possibilities. However, in December 2004, the FDA issued a warning to Barr Pharmaceuticals regarding their television advertisements for Seasonale. The FDA stated that the ads were misleading because they minimized or omitted the risks associated with Seasonale, such as irregular vaginal bleeding or spotting, despite clinical evidence demonstrating its effectiveness in preventing pregnancy. Seasonale is produced by Duramed Pharmaceuticals, a subsidiary of Barr Pharmaceuticals. Its generic version, Quasense, is manufactured by Watson Pharmaceuticals. Each active pill in Seasonale contains 30 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol and 150 micrograms of levonorgestrel. Seasonale reduces the frequency of menstrual periods from thirteen per year to four per year by extending the active pill regimen from 21 days to 84 days. Each package includes 84 active pills and 7 placebo pills to be taken at the end of the active cycle. Seasonique, also produced by Duramed Pharmaceuticals, has a similar packaging and active pill composition to Seasonale but replaces the placebo week with a low-dosage estrogen week. Lybrel, produced by Wyeth Pharmaceuticals, contains 90 micrograms of levonorgestrel and 20 micrograms of ethinyl estradiol in each pill. It is designed to be taken continuously without any placebo pills. Seasonale was first developed by Barr Pharmaceuticals in collaboration with Eastern Virginia Medical School. The FDA approved Seasonale on September 5, 2003. At the time of its approval, Barr Pharmaceuticals stated that Seasonale would cost approximately one dollar per pill. Seasonale is one of 22 oral contraceptive products offered by Barr Pharmaceuticals. The FDA approved Lybrel for human use on May 22, 2007, and it was expected to become available to the public in the United States by July 2007.
